summary: Presents an object-oriented information model for representing policy information, developed with the DMTF's Common Information Model. It gives a common vocabulary for describing rules that govern network behavior. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: This is a shared set of building blocks for writing down network rules, like if this, then do that, so different tools describe them the same way.

questions: what is the policy core information model
what is a policy rule in pcim
how do policy conditions work in dnf and cnf
subtitle: A shared object model for writing down network policy as rules made of conditions and actions.

tldr.problem: Every vendor and tool described network policy (who gets which service, when, and under what circumstances) in its own way, so policies could not be shared or reused.
tldr.mechanism: PCIM defines a small set of object classes: policy groups hold policy rules, and each rule ties a set of conditions to a set of actions, with priorities, roles and time periods to control when it applies.
tldr.outcome: It is a generic information model, not a protocol or a data format. It must be mapped to a concrete data model such as an LDAP schema before it can be implemented, and RFC 3460 later updated it.

today: RFC 3060 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 3460. It is an information model only, and the RFC says it must be mapped to a concrete data model before it can be implemented.

sections.title: What PCIM Is For
sections.content:
The Policy Core Information Model (PCIM) is an object-oriented model for representing policy information. It was developed jointly in the IETF Policy Framework working group and as an extension to the Common Information Model (CIM) of the Distributed Management Task Force (DMTF).

The model defines two hierarchies of classes. Structural classes represent policy information and the control of policies. Association classes say how instances of the structural classes relate to each other. Later documents are expected to map the model onto concrete implementations, for example a directory accessed with LDAPv3.

The classes are generic enough to describe policies about anything, but the RFC expects the first uses in the IETF to be QoS (DiffServ and IntServ) and IPSec. Those areas are meant to extend the core model by subclassing conditions and actions.
sections.eli5: Imagine every school writing its rules in a different language. PCIM is one common rulebook format, so everyone can read each other's rules.

sections.title: Policies, Rules and Groups
sections.content:
The RFC suggests thinking of a policy-controlled network as a state machine, with policy controlling which state a device is in or is allowed to be in. A policy rule is an if-then pair: a set of conditions says when the rule applies, and a set of actions is executed when the conditions evaluate to TRUE. Rules can be collected into policy groups, and groups can be nested to form a hierarchy. A group holds either rules or other groups, but not both.

Rules can be prioritized. The RFC's example: one rule gives engineering traffic Bronze Service, and a second rule with a higher priority gives traffic from one named engineer Gold Service. Both rules match that engineer, and the higher priority settles the conflict. Larger Priority values win and the default is 0.

The model is declarative rather than procedural. It standardizes the building blocks and leaves the algorithms for evaluating them to the implementer. Policies are also categorized with keywords such as CONFIGURATION, USAGE, SECURITY, SERVICE, MOTIVATIONAL, INSTALLATION and EVENT, carried in the PolicyKeywords property.
sections.eli5: A rule says: if it is raining, take an umbrella. A group is a folder of related rules, and folders can sit inside other folders. If two rules disagree, the one with the bigger priority number wins.

sections.title: The Class and Association Hierarchy
sections.content:
Everything descends from the CIM class ManagedElement through the abstract class Policy. Beneath it sit PolicyGroup, PolicyRule, the abstract PolicyCondition and the abstract PolicyAction. PolicyTimePeriodCondition and VendorPolicyCondition are conditions, and VendorPolicyAction is an action. PolicyRepository, a container for reusable policy information, descends from AdminDomain instead.

In CIM, relationships are classes too. The aggregations PolicyGroupInPolicyGroup, PolicyRuleInPolicyGroup, PolicyConditionInPolicyRule, PolicyRuleValidityPeriod and PolicyActionInPolicyRule express whole-part links. Other associations tie groups, rules and repositories to the System that hosts them. Nesting of groups, and of repositories, is assumed to form directed acyclic graphs and not rings.

A condition or action can be rule-specific (created for one rule) or reusable (kept in a repository and shared). The difference is the administrator's intent, not the current associations, and it affects naming and access control rather than the class itself.

Many other associations are inherited from CIM. The RFC's advice is to ignore them unless you need them, for example to attach statistics to a rule.
sections.eli5: Think of a family tree for kinds of things: Policy is the grandparent, and rules, groups, conditions and actions are its children. Other lines show which pieces belong inside which.

sections.title: Conditions: AND Lists and OR Lists
sections.content:
A rule's conditions are combined in one of two standard shapes. In disjunctive normal form (DNF, the default) the conditions form an OR of AND lists. In conjunctive normal form (CNF) they form an AND of OR lists. The rule's ConditionListType property picks the form (DNF(1) or CNF(2)).

Each link between a rule and a condition carries two properties. GroupNumber says which list the condition belongs to, and ConditionNegated says whether it is used as NOT C. With C1, C2, C3 in group 1 (C2 negated) and C4, C5 in group 2, DNF reads as (C1 AND (NOT C2) AND C3) OR (C4 AND C5), and CNF reads as (C1 OR (NOT C2) OR C3) AND (C4 OR C5).

Actions can be ordered with ActionOrder on the link between rule and action. Smaller numbers go earlier, 0 means do not care, and equal non-zero numbers may run in any order. The rule's SequencedActions property says whether that order is mandatory(1), recommended(2) or dontCare(3), the default. Other rule properties include Enabled (enabled(1), disabled(2) or enabledForDebug(3), which evaluates conditions but skips the actions) and Mandatory, which defaults to TRUE.
sections.eli5: A rule can say: do this if (A and B) or (C and D). Each condition is a yes-or-no question, and the lists decide how the answers are combined before the actions happen.

sections.title: Roles and Role Combinations
sections.content:
Instead of configuring thousands of resources one by one, an administrator assigns each resource one or more roles and writes policy for each role. Changing a role's policy once updates every resource that plays it. A role works as a selector that picks a small set of policies out of a very large repository.

Roles can be combined. The PolicyRoles property on a rule holds strings of the form RoleName&&RoleName, with role names in alphabetical order. The names in one string are ANDed, and the multiple values of the property are ORed. A resource in the combination branch-office, Ethernet and WAN picks up policies for all seven non-empty sub-combinations of those roles, so a policy decision point expands the one combination it receives into those seven lookups.

An administrator can declare roles such as Campus and WAN incompatible. Then a resource or rule using both can be flagged as an error, and two rules tied to those roles need not be checked for conflicts with each other.
sections.eli5: Instead of telling every kid in school what to do, you say: all the Year 5 kids do this, and all the choir kids do that. A kid in both groups follows both sets of instructions.

sections.title: Time Periods and Masks
sections.content:
A PolicyTimePeriodCondition says when a rule is valid. It has up to five time properties whose values are ANDed: TimePeriod, MonthOfYearMask, DayOfMonthMask, DayOfWeekMask and TimeOfDayMask. A missing property means always enabled, and a rule with no time period is valid at all times.

  • TimePeriod uses the iCalendar form yyyymmddThhmmss/yyyymmddThhmmss, with THISANDPRIOR and THISANDFUTURE allowed as open ends.
  • MonthOfYearMask is an octet string of size 2: 12 month bits and 4 zero bits.
  • DayOfMonthMask is an octet string of size 8: 31 bits counting from the start of the month, 31 counting from the end, and 2 zero bits.
  • DayOfWeekMask is 1 octet, Sunday first. The value X'7C' means Monday through Friday.
  • TimeOfDayMask is Thhmmss/Thhmmss, and a second time earlier than the first means the range spans midnight.

All the times in one instance are either local time or UTC, chosen by LocalOrUtcTime (localTime(1) or utcTime(2), the default). Named time zones are deliberately left out. A management tool converts them to UTC once, rather than every decision point doing it. That can mean several condition instances for one real schedule, because the offset of US Eastern Time changes with daylight saving. Several time periods linked to one rule through PolicyRuleValidityPeriod are ORed.
sections.eli5: It is like a school timetable for a rule: only on Mondays, only between 8 and 12, only in term time. The rule sleeps the rest of the time.

sections.title: Vendor Extensions
sections.content:
Two classes give vendors a place to put conditions and actions the model does not describe. VendorPolicyCondition has a multi-valued Constraint property and VendorPolicyAction has a multi-valued ActionData property. Both hold octet strings whose format is not specified by the RFC.

The format is named by an object identifier stored as a string in ConstraintEncoding or ActionEncoding, for example 1.2.100.200. A policy decision point checks that identifier against the ones it recognizes. What to do with an unrecognized one could itself be modeled as a policy rule. Standardized extensions are not expected to use these classes.

Other extensions are meant to subclass PolicyCondition and PolicyAction. Documents that subclass PCIM classes SHOULD define extra keywords to characterize their instances.
sections.eli5: It is a blank box with a label on the lid. The label says what language the note inside is written in, so only readers who know that language open it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
PCIM is not a protocol and defines no implementation, so the RFC says it has no specific security requirements of its own. It gives three reasons the model cannot be implemented directly: it is independent of any repository and access protocol, independent of any policy domain, and an information model that must be mapped to a data model first.

Security requirements MUST instead be defined for each real-world application of PCIM. Any that are not handled in an information model document MUST be handled in the derived data model documents. As an illustration, a system giving Gold Service to one person would need data integrity for the policy values, authentication and authorization for administrators, and authentication so the right people get the right service.
sections.eli5: This is a blueprint, not a finished building. Locks and alarms have to be added by whoever builds each real house from it.
